title: Burning or burying? The safer path for Montgomery County’s waste based on the science
summary: The question of what to do with Montgomery County's trash is complicated, but when all factors are weighed, writes Lauren Greenberger, the best solution is to move away from incineration and toward a combination of trash reduction and landfilling.
content:
by Lauren Greenberger, Maryland Matters January 11, 2026

by Lauren Greenberger, Maryland Matters January 11, 2026

Montgomery County is about to make one of the most important environmental and public health decisions in decades: How to manage our municipal solid waste, whether to continue burning it at the Dickerson incinerator or transition to sending it to a vetted regional landfill.

This choice will shape our public health, climate goals, environmental justice commitments and the county’s ability to reduce total waste for years to come.

To make the best decision, we need a full and accurate picture of the impacts. The recent Friends of Sligo Creek report (SCR) presents only part of that picture and overlooks key facts. Having worked with the county as a community advocate for over 10 years, I hope to clarify those gaps so we can choose the option that does the least harm.

Solid waste management is complex. Responsible decisions require accurate comparisons of risks and benefits, something the SCR did not provide. I contributed to a comprehensive report  – Beyond Incineration – commissioned by the county executive that evaluated all available waste management options using a peer-reviewed life cycle analysis (MEBCalc) with public health and environmental justice criteria to identify the least-harm option. Many of the SCR’s conclusions do not align with those findings. Find a point-by-point review of this report here.

The SCR notes that the incinerator meets all but one EPA limit for emissions. This is not accurate. First, with regard to greenhouse gases, there are NO limits on carbon dioxide from incinerators in federal regs and there are no scrubbers in place.

Regarding toxic emissions, our incinerator not only exceeds the EPA limits for hydrogen chloride, it produces more than double the nitrogen oxides that any new incinerator would have to meet. Even more alarmingly, a Nov. 11 report by the incinerator operator, Reworld, revealed that the annual stack test showed dioxin and furan levels nearly double EPA limits. These are two of the deadliest substances known to science – there is no safe established limit. These toxins could have been streaming undetected into our airshed for the past 12 months.

For the rest, “meeting limits” does not mean our incinerator’s emissions are safe. The report relies on older studies to suggest the incinerator’s toxic emissions pose “negligible” health risk. Current health science recognizes the danger of cumulative exposure from multiple pollution sources.

The SCR also does not compare the incinerator directly to modern landfills. Our incinerator emits far more toxic pollutants — including mercury, dioxins, sulfur dioxide, arsenic, beryllium, lead, nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter — than the landfills evaluated in the county’s study.

On environmental justice, the report raises concerns about landfills nationally but does not note that the Montgomery County report evaluated 42 regional landfills and found five that met every equity and performance criterion. We emit approximately 600,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (CO2e) annually. The top 10 landfills the Beyond Incineration report vetted emit an average of half that, much of which is methane. Gas capture rates would have to go as low as 30% for CO2e to be close to the incinerator’s. With health and environmental impacts added, not just climate impacts, incineration is still worse than landfilling even if there is 0% gas capture (see chart here).

The SCR also suggests keeping waste disposal “close to home.” While proximity can matter, it should not outweigh health and safety. The incinerator’s emissions affect communities near the facility and downwind. We send more than 150,000 tons of toxic ash each year to a majority-Black community outside Richmond, Virginia. Ceasing incineration would end this burden for both communities.

Vetted landfills pose the lowest pollution and toxic exposure risks for both Montgomery County and the receiving community.

Notably, Montgomery County is not planning to rely on landfilling alone. The county is already piloting countywide food-scrap composting and Save-As-You-Throw pricing. These strategies will significantly reduce the volume of waste ultimately buried. Thus, landfilling is part of a structured transition to significantly reduce waste overall and reduce costs. A Department of Environmental Protection report in July showed that moving to straight landfill will have slightly increased costs in the first year, but over the following years costs will drop considerably.

After years of study, the county concluded that closing the incinerator and using well-vetted landfills while expanding waste-reduction programs reduces toxic emissions, lowers climate impacts, protects vulnerable communities and aligns with long-term sustainability goals. I applaud our county leaders for moving toward a solution based on current science, best practices in waste management, modern health research, and a commitment to fairness for all communities touched by our waste disposal system.
